item.title: Aaron Rodgers NFL career seems over but three teams could consider quarterback as a late-season option
item.description: Aaron Rodgers says "not how I thought it would end" as the Steelers cut him hours after his Pat McAfee Show interview, leaving his NFL future unclear.
item.content:encoded:
The claims Aaron Rodgers made about Mike McCarthy on national television Wednesday undoubtedly got him cut by the Pittsburgh Steelers and now the question that remains is whether they ended his NFL career.

"Not how I thought it would end," Rodgers said on his now viral interview on the "Pat McAfee Show."

Everyone agrees.

AARON RODGERS NOT RETURNING TO STEELERS, SAYS MIKE MCCARTHY FALLS ASLEEP IN MEETINGS AND IS 'UNWELL'

"... If that's his final ride, you know what I mean, it's probably not the most ideal way to go out," said Raiders pass rusher Maxx Crosby when told of the news. "You don't want to see anyone go out like this."

Rodgers going scorched Earth on McCarthy turned off some executives around the league who shared their feelings with OutKick throughout the day Wednesday. But, interestingly, not everyone believes Rodgers effectively ended his own career because of what he said.

Several executives said they expect "some team" will consider or have internal discussions about signing the soon-to-be 43-year-old quarterback if he clears waivers by Thursday's 4 p.m. deadline.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Rodgers being subject to waivers means any team can claim him by the deadline. Any team that claims Rodgers would have to pay him the remaining portion of his guaranteed salary, which is approximately $8.6 million.

As a practical matter, no team will be claiming Rodgers unless it has an understanding he would report. And Rodgers isn't going to report just anywhere, especially not a losing team with nothing to play for.

But if Rodgers goes unclaimed, he becomes a free agent able to sign with any team he chooses, and he might be tempted to play if a team interests him.

Then the intrigue would begin.

While most teams will not be interested, there are maybe three teams that saw Rodgers on Wednesday's personnel notice and had to at least give thought to adding him the final six weeks of the season and perhaps into the playoffs.

Maybe.

A quick survey of NFL executives Wednesday leads us to those teams:

JALEN HURTS TO REPORTEDLY MISS REMAINDER OF NFL SEASON AFTER BLOOD CLOTS FOUND IN QUARTERBACK'S LUNGS

This is where we admit all of this is speculative because no source on the Patriots, Eagles, or Ravens is saying anything about Rodgers on Wednesday.

But do these teams make sense on some level?

Yes.

The Eagles – They are 3-7 and in last place in the NFC East after losing multiple starters to trades, retirement, and injuries, with starting quarterback Jalen Hurts leading that cast with his season-ending blood clots situation.

The Eagles have started Tanner McKee and lately have turned the offense over to Joe Milton. But it's a mess.

They might decide its a salvageable mess with Rodgers because the division-leading Giants have games scheduled against the 49ers, Lions, Seahawks, and yes, the Eagles in the season-finale. A record under .500 might still win that division.

The Ravens – This is admittedly a long shot. They're hoping they can get Lamar Jackson back from his broken and dislocated right thumb very late in the season and in the meantime they're hoping Jacoby Brissett can keep them in the playoff hunt.

The problem is Brissett is 0-2 as the starter. So would the Ravens believe Rodgers is better? Definitely. But would Rodgers consider trying to rescue a team for a few weeks merely to turn it over to Jackson?

Hard to imagine.

The New England Patriots – Like the other two, they lost their starting quarterback to an injury. Drake Maybe has a ankle or leg fracture, depending on what report one believes, and his return is highly doubtful before the end of the regular season.

But the Patriots have remained in the playoff hunt and their 5-5 record is just one game behind the Steelers. So might they see Rodgers as a boost? And might Rodgers see them as a chance to rally a team that last season went to the Super Bowl?

Again, improbable. But not impossible.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

item.title: CENTCOM's Thanksgiving message to troops 'is one of deep gratitude' for their 'exceptional work' protecting US
item.description: CENTCOM spokesman Tim Hawkins told Fox News Digital that the military command is "grateful" for the family members of American forces positioned overseas.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Central Command spokesperson and Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins told Fox News Digital that his message to the more than 50,000 service members stationed across the Middle East this Thanksgiving is "one of deep gratitude for the exceptional work they're doing."

"Right now, they're focused on a variety of missions, including helping protect shipping moving through the Strait of Hormuz, an international waterway. They're also maintaining America's ironclad blockade against Iran. Highly effective," Hawkins said. "And they're also protecting America and Americans from terrorists. So a lot of hard work. We're very grateful for their outstanding focus, commitment, and dedication to the mission."

Hawkins also said CENTCOM is "grateful" this holiday for the families of America's men and women in uniform.

"We have a highly motivated team deployed to the Middle East, but as many of us know in uniform, military service does not come without great personal service, great personal sacrifice, and great personal cost. And that cost isn't just unique to our service members, it is also shared by the family members back at home who are waiting," Hawkins told Fox News Digital.

'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS

"They're praying. They are holding down the home front during a very, very challenging period of time," he added. "So I want all of them watching to know they are in our thoughts, and we are also grateful to them, and we wish them a happy Thanksgiving."

CENTCOM has played a key role in Operation Epic Fury against Iran, which was launched on Feb. 28.

"Of course, a lot of folks focus on Iran, and that has been a primary focus, but we've been doing other things, continuing to ensure that ISIS doesn't reconstitute in order to protect America and Americans," Hawkins said about the Islamic State terrorist group.

US MILITARY COMPLETES WITHDRAWAL OF TROOPS FROM IRAQ AFTER 12-YEAR MISSION

CENTCOM said in September, following the departure of U.S. forces and equipment in Iraq, "Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve (CJTF-OIR) remains operational and is now headquartered in Jordan as U.S. forces continue the counter-ISIS mission in Syria alongside Coalition partners and the Syrian government."

"We've also been working shoulder to shoulder with our partners and defending against Iranian aggression," Hawkins told Fox News Digital. "There have been around 10,000 or more projectiles fired at innocent civilians, Gulf neighbors, and our service members have stood shoulder to shoulder with our regional partners and protecting not only our forces, but the civilians around.

"And of course, as you have seen in the Strait of Hormuz, traffic is flowing through, and that's because of the great commitment of our service members in protecting international shipping," he added.

item.title: Trump country cracked: 5 races that saw double-digit Trump territory fall to Democrats in 2026
item.description: Donald Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points, yet Scott Colom beat Cindy Hyde-Smith by less than one, ending a 44-year GOP Senate drought.
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points in 2024. Two years later, Democrat Scott Colom won the state’s Senate race, ending a Republican hold that had lasted more than four decades.

Colom’s victory was part of a string of Democratic breakthroughs during the midterms in places Trump had carried by double digits. Democrats also won Senate races in Kansas and South Carolina, captured the Texas governor’s office and flipped a Republican-held House seat deep in Trump country in Indiana that had not elected a Democrat since 1990.

The results stand out for more than the presidential margins as well — Democrats broke Senate streaks that had lasted decades and defeated Republican incumbents in races many expected the GOP to hold, including one where the Democratic challenger spent next to nothing on television advertisements.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE

Here are five of the year’s most striking upsets:

Trump carried the state by nearly 23 points in 2024, and a Democrat had not won a U.S. Senate race in Mississippi since 1982. Several major election forecasters rated the contest Solid Republican for much of the cycle, before shifting it to Likely Republican as the race tightened.

Colom, a district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., by less than one percentage point, 49.36% to 48.54%, according to Associated Press election results. Hyde-Smith had Trump’s backing, and the president rallied for her in the campaign’s final days. Meanwhile, the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, made a seven-figure late-campaign ad buy, as previously reported by Fox News Digital.

The Associated Press did not call the race until Nov. 11, more than a week after Election Day. Colom will also become the first Black senator to represent Mississippi since Reconstruction.

The margin was razor-thin, but the political barrier was enormous — a Trump +23 state, a Trump-backed incumbent and a 44-year drought in Democratic Senate victories. But Democrats pulled off the upset.

Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative, defeated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, R-Texas, as he sought an unprecedented fourth term, ending a 36-year Democratic losing streak in Texas governor’s races. Trump had carried the state by 13.7 points in 2024, according to Associated Press election data, and an October Fox News poll showed Abbott ahead leading up to the Nov. 3 election. Hinojosa, however, ultimately won with 52.8% of the vote to Abbott’s 45.7%, according to Associated Press election results.

Her victory was a major break from Texas’ recent political history and a miss by many major polls. It also made Hinojosa the state’s first Latina governor. Democrats had not won the governor’s office since Ann Richards’ 1990 victory.

Hinojosa’s win was one of two Democratic statewide breakthroughs in Texas, as Democratic state Rep. James Talarico also defeated Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Senate race.

CHUCK DEVORE: TEXAS TURNS BLUE, BUT HERE’S WHERE THE NEXT 4 BIG BATTLES ARE COMING

South Carolina had not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1998, when Fritz Hollings won his final term, and Trump carried the state by nearly 18 points in 2024, according to Associated Press election data. Andrews, a Democratic pediatrician who had never held elected office before, defeated appointed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, by nearly five points.

Graham had Trump’s endorsement and the president also helped her with late campaign appearances on the trail. She had been appointed to serve out her brother’s term after his death, then won the Republican nomination for a full six-year term.

Andrews’ win broke a nearly three-decade Republican hold on the state’s Senate seat and became a rare moment when a Trump-backed candidate lost in a state Republicans had long counted on.

Kansas had not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932, when George McGill won a full term. Hamilton, a Democrat and the founding pastor of a large United Methodist church, defeated first-term Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in a state Trump carried by 16 points in 2024, according to election data from the Associated Press.

The Kansas race was long viewed as a Republican hold, but major election forecasters moved it into toss-up territory late in the campaign as Marshall faced scrutiny over his residency and lawsuits his former medical practice filed against patients.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance both campaigned for Marshall, and Republican-aligned groups spent heavily to keep the seat, including more than $26 million committed to ads supporting him after the August primary — more than was spent on Marshall during his first race in 2020, according to AdImpact data cited by the Associated Press.

Hamilton’s win ended a 94-year Republican Senate streak.

Democrat J.D. Ford defeated three-term Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, which Trump carried by about 17 points, according to Associated Press election results from 2024. Spartz had won re-election there by 18.6 points in 2024, and the district had not elected a Democrat since 1990, when Jim Jontz won.

Ford, a Democratic state senator, won 51.7% to Spartz’s 48.3%, according to the Associated Press results after the midterms. His victory was the only Indiana House seat to change parties, making it a sharp reversal in a state that Trump carried by 19 points statewide in 2024.

Democrats also flipped several other Republican-held House seats in districts Trump carried by double digits, including in North Carolina. Democrat Richard Ojeda defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C., who chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee, the House GOP’s campaign and fundraising arm. Hudson was charged with helping protect the Republican majority, and he had raised $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million and won the district by nearly 19 points in 2024, while Trump had carried it by 16 points.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

In North Carolina’s 6th District, Democrat Cyril Jefferson defeated first-term Rep. Addison McDowell, R-N.C., in a district Trump carried by nearly 17 points, and Democrat Zach Dembo also flipped an open, Republican-held seat in Kentucky’s 6th District, beating Republican Ralph Alvarado by 9.4 points in a district Trump had carried by roughly 15 points in 2024.

Meanwhile, a razor-thin margin in Tennessee’s 4th District underscores the challenges Republicans faced across several traditionally safe districts. Democrat Victoria Broderick, who spent under $100,000 and had no record of airing any paid TV ads, leads incumbent Rep. Scott DesJarlais, R-Tenn., by 277 votes in the latest count, and DesJarlais conceded the race on Nov. 16. Fox News Digital previously reported that Broderick spent under $100,000 compared to DesJarlais’ more than $500,000. The Associated Press has yet to formally call the race with 99% of the vote counted so far.

item.title: Holiday scammers hook older Americans first, then return later to drain their savings, expert warns
item.description: Scammers target older Americans with recovery scams and AI deepfakes during the holidays, hitting victims nine times on average, federal authorities warn.
item.content:encoded:
As the holiday season gets underway, scammers are targeting older Americans with costly schemes that could deplete their entire life savings, often returning to exploiting the same victim more than once.

The risk of elders falling victim to these schemes rises during the holidays. A November 2026 U.S. Secret Service public advisory shared with Fox News Digital stated that scammers consider the season one of their most profitable times of the year.

"USSS is better known for its protective mission," USSS Investigative Analyst Bre Whalen, CFE, told Fox News Digital. "Most people are unaware USSS conducts FI crimes investigations throughout the world, such as Operation Maple Star. Because of its partnerships with the banking community, we've developed close contacts over time." 

Federal authorities warn that scammers exploit the holiday rush and heightened emotions as older adults shop online, track packages online, travel and donate to charities.

An AARP holiday survey released in November found that 84% of U.S. adults had encountered a scam or fraud attempt ahead of the holidays. Nearly 39% of those who purchased something through an online advertisement said they were scammed, according to the survey. Around 47% received fake package-delivery alerts, while 35% bought or received a gift card with a stolen balance.

Americans ages 60 and older reported around $3 billion in fraud losses in 2025, according to an October 2026 Federal Trade Commission report. The agency estimated that older victims lost as much as $119.5 billion last year, with victims reporting only a fraction of the scams.

AGING MEANS LEARNING HOW TO PREVENT COSTLY SCAMS TARGETING OLDER AMERICANS

The Justice Department reports that scammers target older Americans an average of nine times. After taking money in an initial scheme, fraudsters often contact victims again, posing as officials promising to recover their funds.

"Criminals will go back to where the money is," Amy Nofziger, senior director of fraud victim support at AARP's Fraud Watch Network, told Fox News Digital.

WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE

"It's just why some banks get robbed every single time — the same bank — because the criminals go where the money is, and older adults hold the majority of wealth in the United States."

The process can still be challenging, experts said. Winning the confidence of victims can be difficult after they’ve been targeted and scammed. 

"Victims don't trust or believe what we're saying because they've been coached by these scam centers to not answer law enforcement and think we're not real," Whalen stated.

The Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said that after a successful scam, some fraudsters will share victims' personal information on the black market. This allows other criminals to target the same person, but with different schemes.

A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?

For instance, when an older shopper places an order for a fake Black Friday ad or donates to a fraudulent holiday charity site, scammers take their information and place them on "sucker lists." The lists mark these victims as easy targets, with repeated attacks that could ultimately wipe out their life savings.

"Criminals are very adept at sharing information," Nofziger said. "A lot of these criminals don't work in isolation. They work in crime rings. Perhaps Criminal A steals from a victim on a Monday, and then five Mondays later, they give or sell that information to Criminal B to try to manipulate them on another scam, knowing they still might have resources available to steal."

FAKE FEDERAL AGENTS PUSH SENIORS TO TURN SAVINGS INTO GOLD BARS FOR COURIERS TO COLLECT

Promises to recover stolen money or lost funds are one of the most damaging schemes to older Americans during the holiday season.

After a victim loses money, another scammer may call and claim to work for a government agency, or pose as an attorney or a fraud-recovery investigator. The caller then promises to investigate the crime, find the money and get a refund.

SCAMMERS ARE COMING FOR YOUR MONEY. HERE’S THE ONE THING YOU MUST NEVER DO

Fraudsters will also exploit tax and financial deadlines while pushing victims to wire an immediate "processing fee" before Dec. 31 to recover lost funds or unlock a refund.

Federal authorities warn that legitimate agencies never require upfront fees to recover stolen funds, but victims often fall prey to these schemes when they become outraged and want swift justice.

"For the initial victim, they're so angry, they're so upset, they want to get justice for this," Nofziger said. "They think that this is their way out, oftentimes not really understanding that it's just a secondary scam that's happening."

Scammers are exploiting holiday fears with AI-generated emergency calls that mimic relatives and payment-app requests designed to steal money.

One scheme, known as the "grandparent scam," happens when criminals pull videos from social media accounts or public sources. They clone a relative's voice using artificial intelligence, and then pose as loved ones asking for emergency funds or Christmas cash.

Fraudsters are also using full AI video deepfakes, sometimes posing as physicians, to bilk funds from unsuspecting older Americans.

In December 2025, an 82-year-old Florida grandmother lost more than $200,000 to an AI deepfake scam, when someone pretended to be a doctor in a Facebook community focused on autism.

The grandmother said she had been saving her money for her autistic grandson’s future, and the fake physician urged people to invest.

"It looked completely real — his face, his voice, everything," she told First Coast News. "I wanted to save more money for my grandson, and so I fell for it hook, line and sinker."

"I got very emotional and so angry with myself that I had difficulty functioning. I lost 20 pounds and couldn’t sleep because it went through my mind over and over again."

Shame can keep victims silent, which ends up leaving them vulnerable to repeat attacks, Nofziger said, adding that victims may feel guilt for being scammed in the first place.

Nofziger urges families to discuss these scams openly, while taking steps to avoid victim-blaming.

"The scammers are masters of manipulation, and they know how to manipulate human beings and their feelings," she said. "The victim has been manipulated and technically, you know, brainwashed by this criminal for months and years."

"It took years to get there. It might take a long time to unravel that emotional grasp that these criminals have on their victims... The person who should be embarrassed is the criminal who stole the money from them."

She added that unraveling a scammer's manipulative hold takes time and outside support, whether from local law enforcement, support groups or counselors.

SEND US A TIP

Victims are urged to contact their banks, payment providers, and local law enforcement immediately if they suspect fraud. Banks can possibly stop or recall some transfers, but it largely depends on the payment method and how quickly they report the scam.

GOT A TIP?

Cryptocurrency, gift cards, cash and gold are more difficult to recover since criminals typically know how to move them quickly. Once a victim is ensnared, scammers can move the money through multiple accounts and intermediaries, such as money mules, to hide transactions.

USSS advises victims to immediately report any suspected fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"Current fraud info is provided real time; in most cases we have just minutes to act on this information before the fraud is committed," Whalen said. 

"We work closely with local police and banking industry, although we are still working to make efforts to partner with some of the banking sector that is slow to respond to real-time data."

Anyone of any age, including non-members, can contact the free AARP Fraud Watch Network Helpline at 877-908-3360 for guidance, support groups and to learn about other steps to take.

Victims and families can also contact the National Elder Fraud Hotline at 833-FRAUD-11 or visit the Justice Department’s Elder Justice Initiative website.

item.title: Miles for Military program turns volunteer work into flights home for service members
item.description: Marine Cpl. Dominic Morimando surprised his mom for the holidays by running PE at Spotswood Elementary, earning a ticket home via Miles for Military.
item.content:encoded:
After more than a year apart, Marine Cpl. Dominic Morimando surprised his mother with a visit home for the holidays through a program that allows service members to earn flights home by volunteering.

He told "Fox & Friends Weekend" on Sunday that the enthusiasm of the students he worked with made the experience rewarding.

"It was such a great experience because they are so excited and so happy to have us there, and I was able to accumulate so many hours," the corporal said.

He volunteered at Spotswood Elementary School, working with students in kindergarten through fifth grade during physical education classes.

U.S. AIR FORCE MOM SURPRISES FAMILY ON TURF AT VIKINGS-BILLS GAME FOLLOWING 473-DAY OVERSEAS DEPLOYMENT

Dominic's mother, Ivonne Morimando, said she was "very, very proud" of her son. She recalled her surprise at seeing him standing at her front door.

"My heart was – I still have that emotion in front of me because just seeing him right in the front door, it was a big thing for me, for real."

"It's so much fun and happiness to have him over here with us, especially in these days, this holiday," she said.

Dominic's trip was made possible by Miles for Military, a nonprofit that provides flights home to U.S. service members in exchange for volunteer work.

Founder Maureen Byrne, whose son served in the Marines, told Fox News she chose the community service model instead of simply providing free flights so that service members could "get off base, get into community, do something, learn something, have fun."

"It's so rewarding. I was talking to [Dominic] when I was in Las Vegas yesterday about his volunteer work and he lit up talking about the kids."

TUNNEL TO TOWERS PAYS OFF MORTGAGES FOR 30 MILITARY FAMILIES IN VETERANS DAY TRIBUTE: 'A GREAT SACRIFICE'

Byrne said her son's positive experience volunteering, along with the high cost of flying home, helped inspire Miles for Military.

"The ticket was almost $900 from Camp Lejeune to Boston."

The high cost prompted her to ask her son how other service members paid for trips home.

"'Mom, they don't. Nobody gets to go home. They can't afford it,'" Byrne recalled her son saying.

"Well, what if we have these kids do some volunteer work and, in exchange, we give them a ticket home? And that's how Miles for Military came."

For Dominic, the value of the program extended beyond the flight home.

Service, he said, is "very important because you're taking your time out of your life to serve not only your country, but your community and everybody else around you as well."

item.title: Meet the mastermind behind New York City's iconic Christmas light displays and holiday magic
item.description: Some of NYC's most popular Christmas decorations at Radio City Music Hall, Macy's and Bloomingdale's get help from one man and his crew every Christmas.
item.content:encoded:
While most of New York City is asleep, dedicated crews are racing against the clock to turn the Big Apple into a holiday wonderland.

"I would say our average projects, probably about 30 people for a night or two," says American Christmas CEO Dan Casterella. 

Casterella is the man behind some of the most popular lighting displays in the tristate area. 

From Macy's, Bloomingdale’s, Saks Fifth Avenue and Radio City Music Hall to the FOX News Christmas Tree, Casterella and his team create the city's signature Christmas magic. 

FOX NEWS KICKS OFF HOLIDAY SEASON WITH CHRISTMAS TREE LIGHTING 

"It's like a once in a lifetime opportunity," Florida mom Kate Rankin tells FOX, "I feel like New York is… unlike anywhere else."

"There’s a tradition of people visiting New York to see the holiday decorations," Casterella says, "I meet people all the time and even some of our clients kind of talk about how they used to do it with their parents when they were kids."

Rankin shares the same story.

"Growing up in Jersey, we did this as a kid," she tells FOX. "So we came all the time. And now that I live in Tampa, I try to bring my children up here so that they can see."

REDDIT USERS SHARE WILDEST THINGS SEEN AT CHRISTMAS PARTIES

To turn a building facade into a dazzling Christmas light show, Casterella says retailers reach out to his team months in advance—sometimes nearly a whole year.

"I would say our entire company is 24 hours," Casterella tells FOX. "And that will continue for the next 10 to 15 days."

American Christmas employs engineers, designers, welders and builders who piece each elaborate concept together.

"We get into January and February, and we start designing and developing from there," Casterella says, "We go into engineering in March, and then in April, orders get placed."

Casterella says that by the end of September, his crews are in full swing hanging up lights and building large-scale decorations.

Once the season wraps up, Casterella says more than 2,500 truckloads of gear will have rolled into town, and more than 400 projects will be finished across the tristate area alone. His team also works nationwide, completing more than 800 projects bearing the American Christmas name by the end of the season.

While losing hours of sleep and working grueling overnight shifts, Casterella says he has always had a passion for Christmas decorations, even telling FOX he would ask for decorations as Christmas gifts.

"I've loved it since I was a kid. I was decorating homes for Christmas when I was a kid. That's how I made money in high school. And I was in college and started working here, and I never left," Casterella says. 

A popular stop decorated by Casterella and his team is Radio City Music Hall. The venue has been a client for over 20 years, and American Christmas crews continue to reimagine the 64-foot tree that is lit with 50,000 LEDs.

As for the FOX News Christmas Tree, Casterella says it took his team 36 hours to build the frame and branches. The tree features 48,000 LEDs and thousands of ornaments wired into the branches to ensure wind or weather does not impact the display.

It takes American Christmas about nine weeks to decorate the Big Apple, with only three weeks to take everything down, starting the day after Christmas.

item.title: Holiday staples still surging ahead of Thanksgiving dinner. Economist shares how to save on the spread
item.description: Diesel costs are driving up meat, dairy and fresh food prices this Thanksgiving, but an expert says brand flexibility can keep meals affordable.
item.content:encoded:
The turkey may be a holiday bargain, but rising prices for meat, dairy and fresh foods could make the rest of the Thanksgiving spread cost much more this year.

Richard Volpe, a professor of agribusiness at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, told Fox News Digital that sustained high energy costs in the midst of the Iran war — particularly for diesel — are pushing up grocery prices just as households prepare to host holiday meals.

Surging prices of ham and eggnog, in particular, could put a damper on some holiday favorites.

"Most of the biggest increases are things like fruits, vegetables and meats," Volpe said. "Fresh and refrigerated foods feel those costs sooner than shelf-stable products."

7 COSTCO THANKSGIVING FOOD DEALS AND STEALS THAT SHOPPERS CAN'T MISS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON

Dairy is also especially energy and transportation intensive, putting holiday staples such as butter and eggnog under pressure.

Volpe said shoppers willing to switch brands and take advantage of store promotions can keep holiday meals more affordable.

"If you are less worried about brand or banner loyalty, and you’re able to follow promotions and look for these sort of aggressive, enticing deals, there are still ways to achieve savings and to keep those Thanksgiving and holiday dinners relatively affordable," Volpe said.

He also acknowledged that high beef and pork prices could contribute to some households deciding to dine on a different main dish for their holiday meals this year.

"Beef and pork are particularly expensive right now, so I would expect to see some substitutions there," he said. "I would strongly suspect that across the country, there are folks who are roasting turkeys and chickens, or even salmon or some other large sort of centerpiece to the meal that’s protein-based other than beef and pork."

AMERICANS ARE MAKING COSTLY GROCERY MISTAKE EVEN BEFORE ENTERING THE STORE, EXPERT WARNS

Swapping the menu may help, but Volpe said skipping the grocery store for a restaurant or catered meal is unlikely to save money.

"It is still cheaper to go to the grocery store and prepare food at home," Volpe said.

He said restaurant prices have risen nearly twice as fast as grocery prices over the past two to two and a half years.

Volpe said he still expects food prices to rise at a more typical pace this year, even as the increases come during the holiday hosting season.

"I'm not expecting food price inflation anything like what we saw in ’21 and ’22," he said. "We’re actually still very likely on track for roughly normal food price inflation on the year."
